card.keepWhy: Waiting, done like that, is a way of watching.
sources: Luke 2:22-38 (after the days of purification they carried him to Jerusalem to present him to the Lord, with a pair of turtledoves or two young pigeons; Simeon, just and devout, waiting for the consolation of Israel; the Holy Ghost had told him he should not see death before he had seen the Christ of the Lord; he came by the Spirit into the temple, took him into his arms and blessed God: “Now thou dost dismiss thy servant, O Lord, according to thy word in peace; because my eyes have seen thy salvation … a light to the revelation of the Gentiles, and the glory of thy people Israel”; to Mary: “thy own soul a sword shall pierce”; Anna, a prophetess, daughter of Phanuel, who had lived with her husband seven years and was a widow until fourscore and four years, who departed not from the temple, by fastings and prayers serving night and day; she confessed to the Lord and spoke of him to all that looked for the redemption of Israel). Douay-Rheims.
Leviticus 12:2-8 (forty days; two turtledoves or two young pigeons if she cannot afford a lamb).
Liturgy of the Hours, Night Prayer: the Canticle of Simeon (Nunc Dimittis). Roman Missal, the Presentation of the Lord, 2 February: blessing of candles and procession (Candlemas).
check: Luke never says Simeon was old; tradition pictures him so, and the painting shows an old man. The caption avoids his age. Confirm.
Anna’s age: “a widow until fourscore and four years” can mean she was 84, or widowed for 84 years. The lesson says “in her eighties”. Confirm.

hook.say: before the story, can i ask you something? what are you waiting for right now: news, a person, a change?
options: i hope it comes. hold it while you watch.
the loading bars of life. watch this man.
that’s okay. this story keeps quiet company too.

steps.line: Forty days after the birth, Mary and Joseph carried the baby to the Temple in Jerusalem with two small birds, the offering of families who couldn’t afford a lamb.
In Jerusalem lived a devout man named Simeon. God had promised he would not die before he saw the Messiah. So he waited, day after day.

steps.q: That day, Simeon feels moved to go to the Temple. What does he do when he sees the baby?
o: Asks the parents who they are
Takes the baby in his arms
steps.why: He takes him in his arms. Luke says the Spirit moved him to come that day, and out of all the families in the courts, he knew.

steps.line: He came into the Temple courts, saw one more young couple in the crowd, and took their baby in his arms. Then he prayed.

steps.q: Simeon’s prayer became one of the Church’s daily prayers. When is it said?
o: At the first Mass of the morning
At noon, with the Angelus bell
Right before sleep, at Night Prayer
steps.why: It’s the Nunc dimittis, Latin for “now you dismiss.” It fits the end of the day: sleep is a small letting go, made in peace.

steps.line: He called the child “a light for the nations, and the glory of your people Israel.” Then, gently, he told Mary a sword would pierce her own soul.
Then came Anna, a prophetess, a widow in her eighties who never left the Temple, praying night and day. She thanked God and spoke of the child to everyone.

steps.q: Most people walked right past one more young couple. Why did Simeon and Anna notice this baby?
o: The Spirit led them, and they were watching
Mary and Joseph had told them who he was
Word from the shepherds had reached the city
steps.why: Luke says the Holy Spirit was upon Simeon and brought him to the Temple that day, and Anna had prayed there for decades. Nothing about the family looked special: two birds was the poor family’s offering.

steps.line: Today, on February 2, Catholics bless candles and carry them in procession, because Simeon called the child a light. Many call it Candlemas.
steps.label: today

steps.q: Candlemas falls on February 2. Why that date?
o: The day Simeon died, by tradition
steps.why: Forty days after December 25: the Law of Moses set forty days of purification for a mother after a son. Groundhog Day lands on the same date.

say: here’s what i love. simeon and anna were jews waiting on israel’s hope, and their waiting wasn’t empty. it was full: prayer, watching, showing up.
that’s why they knew the baby everyone else walked past. the church prays simeon’s words every night at night prayer: now, lord, you let your servant go in peace.

steps.q: Simeon, a devout Jew in the Temple, calls this Jewish baby “a light for the nations.” Who are “the nations”?
o: Every people on earth, not only Israel
The Roman rulers of the land
steps.why: In the Bible “the nations” are the peoples beyond Israel. Simeon echoes Isaiah, where God’s servant is “a light to the nations,” so salvation reaches the ends of the earth.

today.say: today, turn one wait into a watch: in a line, a waiting room, on hold. instead of scrolling, look around, or say one quiet prayer for someone near you. if you pray at night, you can try simeon’s words before sleep.
options: I’ll try it in a line
good. waiting done like that isn’t wasted.
lovely. now, lord, you let your servant go in peace.
